newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German GDP rise doesn't rule out rate cut - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German GDP rise doesn't rule out rate cut - analysts.

text.p: German economic growth in the third quarter outstripped most forecasts, data showed on Wednesday, but analysts said there was still scope for a possible interest rate cut, further bond market gains and a weaker mark.
The Federal Statistics Office said that quarter-on-quarter growth slowed to 1.0 percent in the third quarter after 1.5 percent growth in the spring period.
Year-on-year growth in pan-German gross domestic product (GDP) doubled its pace in the third quarter to 2.4 percent from 1.2 percent in the previous quarter.
Both GDP numbers were at the top of market expectations, initially pushing the mark up a pfennig against the dollar and sparking profit-taking in German government bonds after gains.
"It's a touch stronger than people expected," Rob Hayward at Bank of America said of the data.

But following Tuesday's poor October industrial production data and with jobless figures on Thursday set to show a lengthening of dole queues, analysts cautioned against taking the view that Germany's recovery is firmly established.
"This is just a look into the rear-view mirror, and ahead of us seems to be a rather flat fourth quarter," Adolf Rosenstock at the Industrial Bank of Japan said.
"We need a tremendous increase in November and December just to break even over the third quarter," Rosenstock said. He added that the outlook for early 1997 was "still muted".
Analysts said, however, that a 3.2 percent year-on-year rise in capital investment was good news for a recovery which had previously been driven almost exclusively by exports.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt also said recovery was gaining strength and official forecasts -- of 1.25 percent growth this year and 2.5 percent in 1997 -- could be met.
"There are good prospects for turning the current recovery into a sustained economic upswing," he said.
Rosenstock and Hayward said there was still a chance that the Bundesbank would shave its repo rate, which is now at three percent, in the new year.
But Juergen Pfister at Commerzbank ruled out any further rate reductions. "It's quite clear for now that the economy is on an upward path, but a very slow one," he said.

"We don't see any possibility for a further cut in short-term interest rates as all the Bundesbank's arguments for lower rates -- a weak economy and a stronger mark -- are no longer there," Pfister added.
The stronger growth figures may lead to a slight correction in German bond markets, but Hayward said that the market was still well underpinned.
"I think the bund market is well supported and inflation is well under control," Hayward said. The 10-year bund eased 30 basis points after the data, with the yield up to 5.65 percent.
Pfister said: "We have shifted from a low-growth scenario to a moderate growth scenario, so we expect some change in the bond market -- but in early 1997 rather than sooner."
Economists agreed that the GDP numbers would give a modest boost to the German mark, which rose to 1.5578/82 to the dollar in morning trading from from 1.5665/70 on Tuesday.
But the underlying picture of low interest rates and the prospect of linking up in 1999 with a larger group of weaker currencies in European monetary union (EMU) pointed to mark weakness.
"EMU remains a risk for the mark," Rosenstock said.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
